unit.title: Prepare and cook meat and seafood

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What core temperature should minced meat, such as the beef in patties or burgers, reach (or as the Centre's food safety plan says)?

Vinegar with onion, carrot and hot pepper

questions.stem: Jerk pork must be cooked until it is:

essays.stem: Describe how you would check a delivery of fresh meat and fresh fish, and how you would store each one safely.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the delivery as soon as it arrives. I check the temperature with a clean probe: chilled meat and fish should be at 5 °C or below (or as the Centre's food safety plan says). The packaging must be clean and not torn, and the dates must be right. Fresh meat should have a good colour and a fresh smell, with no slime. Fresh fish should have bright, clear eyes, red or pink gills, firm flesh that springs back, and a fresh sea smell. If anything is wrong, I do not accept it and I tell the supervisor. I put the food away quickly. Raw meat goes covered, labelled and dated in a tray on the bottom shelf of the fridge, below cooked and ready-to-eat food. Fish is kept covered in its own container in the coldest part of the fridge, or on ice that drains away, and is used soon. I put new stock behind old stock (first in, first out) and write the delivery check in the records.
markingPoints: Checks the temperature (5 °C or below), packaging and dates
Quality signs for meat: colour, smell, no slime
Quality signs for fish: eyes, gills, firm flesh, fresh smell; reject and report if wrong
Stores raw meat covered, labelled, on the bottom shelf below ready-to-eat food
Stores fish covered and very cold, uses it soon; first in, first out; records kept

essays.stem: Describe how to scale, gut and clean a whole fish, such as a snapper, ready for frying.
essays.modelAnswer: I set up a clean board, using the Centre's colour for raw fish, on a damp cloth so it cannot slip, and I have a scaler or the back of a knife, a sharp knife, scissors and a bowl for waste. To scale the fish, I hold it by the tail and scrape from the tail towards the head, on both sides, under running water or in a deep sink so the scales do not fly about. I cut off the fins with scissors, taking care with the sharp spines. To gut it, I cut along the belly from the vent to the head, pull out the guts and throw them away. I take out the gills, because they spoil quickly and taste bitter. I wash the inside with cold water and scrape away the dark blood line along the backbone. I score the sides two or three times so the seasoning can go in and the fish cooks evenly. I pat it dry and keep it covered in the fridge until I cook it. Then I clean and sanitise the board, knife, sink and bench.
markingPoints: Safe set-up: correct board on a damp cloth, sharp knife, scaler, waste bowl
Scale from tail to head on both sides; trim fins, watching the spines
Gut through the belly and remove the gills
Wash the cavity and remove the blood line; score the sides
Keep chilled until cooking; clean and sanitise the area afterwards

essays.stem: Describe how to cook escovitch fish, including the escovitch pickle.
essays.modelAnswer: I use a cleaned, scaled and scored whole fish, such as snapper or parrot fish. I season it inside and out with salt and black pepper, and some cooks add a little lime juice. I pat it dry so the oil will not spit. I heat oil in a heavy frying pan and lay the fish in gently, away from me. I fry it on both sides until it is crisp and golden and the flesh near the bone is opaque and flakes easily. I lift it out and drain it on kitchen paper. For the pickle, I slice onion, carrot, sweet pepper and cho cho into thin strips, and slice Scotch bonnet pepper, wearing gloves. I put vinegar in a pan with pimento berries, a little salt and sugar, and bring it to the boil. I add the vegetables and cook them for only a minute or two so they stay crunchy. I pour the hot pickle over the fried fish and serve it with bammy or festival. If it is kept, it goes covered and labelled into the fridge.
markingPoints: Season the cleaned, scored fish and pat it dry
Fry safely in hot oil, laid in away from the body, until crisp and cooked through
Pickle vegetables cut in thin strips; gloves for Scotch bonnet
Vinegar boiled with pimento and seasoning; vegetables cooked briefly so they stay crisp
Pickle poured over the fish; served with bammy or festival; leftovers chilled and labelled

essays.stem: Describe the steps to prepare and cook curry goat.
essays.modelAnswer: I cut the goat into even pieces of about 3–4 cm with a cleaver or heavy knife, on a board that cannot slip, and trim off extra fat. I wash my hands and clean the board after. I season the meat with curry powder, salt, black pepper, garlic, onion, thyme, scallion, Scotch bonnet pepper (using gloves) and pimento. I cover and label it and leave it in the fridge to take in the flavour, best overnight. To cook, I heat oil in a heavy pot and cook a little curry powder in it for a short time to bring out the flavour. I add the meat and brown it, stirring. Then I add water to come part way up the meat, cover the pot, and simmer gently for about 2 hours, or less in a pressure cooker used as the maker says, stirring now and then and adding water if needed. When the meat is nearly tender, I add diced potato to help thicken the gravy. I taste with a clean spoon, adjust the seasoning, and serve it hot with white rice.
markingPoints: Cut the goat into even pieces safely and trim the fat
Season with curry and Jamaican seasonings; marinate covered in the fridge
Cook the curry in hot oil first, then brown the meat
Add liquid, cover and simmer slowly until tender (pressure cooker used as the maker says)
Add potato to thicken; taste with a clean spoon; serve hot with rice

essays.stem: Compare dry-heat and moist-heat cooking for meat. Give a Jamaican example of each, and say which cuts suit each method.
essays.modelAnswer: Dry-heat cooking uses hot air, hot metal or hot oil, with no water. Grilling, roasting, baking and frying are dry-heat methods. They cook quickly and give a brown, tasty outside. A Jamaican example is jerk pork or jerk chicken on a grill, or fried fish. Dry heat suits tender cuts with little connective tissue, such as sirloin steak, pork chops, pork loin and fish, because they soften quickly and would dry out if cooked for a long time. Moist-heat cooking uses liquid or steam. Stewing, braising, boiling, steaming and pressure cooking are moist-heat methods. They cook slowly and gently. Jamaican examples are curry goat, stewed oxtail with butter beans and steamed fish. Moist heat suits tough cuts with a lot of connective tissue, such as oxtail, shin, goat, cow foot and neck, because long, slow cooking in liquid turns the tough tissue into gelatine and makes the meat soft. Fish is the exception: it is tender, so it is steamed only for a short time.
markingPoints: Dry heat: grill, roast, bake, fry; quick, brown outside
Dry heat suits tender cuts (steak, chops, loin, fish)
Moist heat: stew, braise, boil, steam; slow and gentle
Moist heat suits tough cuts (oxtail, goat, shin, cow foot): collagen becomes gelatine
Correct Jamaican example of each (e.g. jerk pork; curry goat, stewed oxtail, steamed fish)

essays.stem: Describe how to check, prepare and cook shrimp for a dish such as pepper shrimp.
essays.modelAnswer: I check shrimp when they arrive. Fresh shrimp are firm and shiny, with a mild sea smell. I reject shrimp that are slimy, soft, have black spots or smell of ammonia. I keep them on ice or in the fridge at 5 °C or below until I use them, and I use a separate board and knife for raw seafood. To prepare them, I may leave the shell on for pepper shrimp, or peel off the shell and legs for other dishes. I devein them by cutting a shallow slit along the back and lifting out the dark gut. I rinse them in cold water and drain them well. For pepper shrimp, I cook the shrimp in a pot with water or a little oil, salt, garlic, Scotch bonnet pepper (handled with gloves), pimento and some annatto or paprika for colour. Shrimp cook quickly: they are ready when they turn pink and firm and the flesh is opaque, usually in a few minutes. I do not overcook them, or they turn tough. I serve them hot or chill them quickly, and I tell guests they contain shellfish, a common allergen.
markingPoints: Checks quality: firm, shiny, mild smell; rejects slimy or ammonia-smelling shrimp
Keeps them chilled at 5 °C or below; separate board for raw seafood
Peels if needed and deveins along the back
Cooks briefly until pink, firm and opaque; does not overcook; gloves for peppers
Serves hot or chills quickly; shellfish allergen made known

essays.stem: Explain how to prepare saltfish so it is ready to cook, and say why each step is done.
essays.modelAnswer: Saltfish is cod or another white fish that has been salted and dried, so it keeps a long time. It is far too salty to eat as it comes. First, I rinse off the loose salt. Then I soak it in cold water, best overnight in the fridge, changing the water two or three times, or I boil it in fresh water, pour off the water and boil it again. This takes out the extra salt. I taste a small cooked piece to check the salt level. Next, I drain the fish and let it cool enough to handle. I remove the skin and all the bones, because bones are a choking risk for guests. Then I flake the flesh into small pieces with my fingers or a fork, so it mixes well with the ackee or other ingredients. If I am not using it straight away, I keep it covered, labelled and dated in the fridge.
markingPoints: Saltfish is salted, dried fish and is too salty to use as it comes
Soak in cold water (changing it) or boil and change the water, to remove salt
Taste to check the salt level
Remove skin and all bones (choking risk)
Flake the fish; store covered, labelled and chilled if not used at once

essays.stem: Describe how to use a pressure cooker safely to cook a tough cut such as oxtail or cow foot.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the maker's instructions and follow the Centre's rules. Before I start, I check that the rubber seal is clean, soft and in place, and that the valve and safety vent are clean and not blocked. I put in the browned meat and liquid, but I never fill the pot above the maximum line the maker marks, because food needs room to boil and foam. I close and lock the lid as the maker says. I heat it until it reaches pressure, then turn the heat down to keep it steady, and time the cooking. I never leave it unattended and I keep my face and hands away from the valve. When the time is up, I turn off the heat and let the pressure drop as the maker says, either by itself or with the release method in the instructions. I never force the lid open; I open it only when all the pressure has gone, tilting the lid away from me so the steam goes the other way. Afterwards I clean the seal, valve and lid.
markingPoints: Follow the maker's instructions; check the seal, valve and vent before use
Never fill above the maximum line
Lock the lid correctly; lower the heat at pressure; never leave it unattended
Release pressure fully as the maker says; never force the lid; open away from the face
Clean the seal, valve and lid after use

essays.stem: Explain how you would serve a guest who says they have a shellfish allergy, from taking the order to serving the dish.
essays.modelAnswer: A shellfish allergy can cause a very serious reaction, so it must be taken seriously every time. When the order is taken, the allergy is written clearly on the order and the server tells the chef. In the kitchen, I check the recipe and the labels of every ingredient, including stocks and sauces, for shrimp, lobster, crab or conch. If I am not sure, I ask the chef and do not guess. I wash my hands and use clean boards, knives, pans, tongs and oil that have not touched shellfish. I cook the dish apart from the shellfish dishes and cover it once it is plated. I mark the plate or give it to the server directly, saying it is the allergy order, so it goes to the right guest. If the kitchen cannot make the dish safely, the guest is told honestly and offered another dish. If a guest shows signs of a reaction, the staff call for help at once and follow the first-aid plan.
markingPoints: Allergy recorded on the order and the chef told
Check recipes and labels of all ingredients; ask, never guess
Clean equipment and separate cooking to avoid cross-contact
Plate marked or handed over directly to reach the right guest
Be honest if it cannot be made safely; know to call for help if a reaction happens

essays.stem: Explain how to cool, store and reheat a large pot of stewed oxtail safely.
essays.modelAnswer: A large pot of stew cools slowly, so it can stay in the danger zone, between 5 °C and 63 °C, for a long time and let bacteria grow. To cool it quickly, I take it off the heat and split it into shallow trays or small containers. I can stand the containers in a sink of iced water and stir now and then. As soon as it has cooled, within the time the Centre's food safety plan gives, I cover it, label it with the name and date, and put it in the fridge at 5 °C or below, above any raw meat. I use it within the time the plan allows. To reheat, I heat only what I need, in a pan, stirring, until the core reaches about 74 °C, checked with a clean probe, and I write the reading down. I reheat it once only, and then keep it hot at about 63 °C or above for service. Any reheated stew that is left over is thrown away.
markingPoints: Explains why a big pot is a risk (slow cooling through the danger zone)
Cool quickly in shallow trays or an ice bath
Cover, label and date; store at 5 °C or below above raw meat
Reheat to about 74 °C core, checked and recorded
Reheat once only; hot-hold at about 63 °C or above; discard leftovers

practical1.title: Curry goat and grilled pork chops: moist-heat and dry-heat cooking
practical1.brief: As a group, prepare and cook curry goat for 8 portions, and grill a pork chop for each member. Each member cuts and trims part of the goat into even pieces with the assessor watching. Together, season the goat and keep it covered and labelled in the fridge (the assessor may give you a batch seasoned the day before to cook). Take turns to cook the curry, brown the meat and stew it until tender, adding potato near the end. While the curry cooks, each member trims, seasons and grills one pork chop, checks that it is cooked through with a clean probe, records the temperature and rests it. Plate 4 portions of curry goat with rice, and each member plates their own pork chop with a garnish. Then clean and sanitise the area. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the plates are done and the area is clean.
materials: About 1.6 kg goat on the bone, and 1 pork chop for each member
Curry powder, onion, garlic, thyme, scallion, Scotch bonnet pepper, pimento, salt, black pepper
Cleaver or heavy knife, cook's knives, boards in the Centre's colour code
Heavy pot with lid, grill or grill pan, tongs, trays
Clean probe thermometer, probe wipes, temperature log sheet
photos: The raw-meat work area set up, with every member in uniform and hair cover
The goat cut into even pieces and trimmed
The seasoned goat in a covered, labelled container
The goat being browned, and then stewing in the pot
Each member's pork chop on the grill, and the probe reading
The finished curry goat plates and each member's pork chop plate
The work area cleaned and sanitised at the end
checklist: Wore a clean uniform and hair cover; washed hands before and after raw meat
Cut the meat into even pieces safely, with the board on a damp cloth
Wore gloves for Scotch bonnet pepper and kept seasoned meat covered in the fridge
Browned and stewed the goat until tender, stirring and checking the liquid
Grilled a pork chop until cooked through, turning it with tongs
Checked and recorded the core temperature with a clean probe
Tasted with a clean spoon, and plated neatly on a warm plate with a clean rim
Cleaned and sanitised boards, knives, pots, grill and work surfaces
safety: Use the cleaver only on a steady board, with fingers well away from the blade
Keep raw meat away from cooked food; use separate tongs for raw and cooked
Turn pan handles inwards; use dry oven cloths for hot pots and grills
Keep a fire blanket near the stove and never leave hot oil or a grill unattended
Wipe up spills at once and put out a wet-floor sign

practical2.title: Clean and fry whole fish for escovitch fish, and prepare pepper shrimp
practical2.brief: As a group, prepare escovitch fish and pepper shrimp. The assessor gives each member one whole fish (such as snapper, about 300–400 g) and a portion of raw shrimp. Each member scales, guts, cleans and scores their own fish, then seasons it. Two members slice the vegetables for the escovitch pickle, wearing gloves for the Scotch bonnet pepper, and two make the pickle. Each member fries their own fish in hot oil with the assessor watching, and checks that it is cooked through. Each member also peels and deveins their portion of shrimp, and the group cooks the pepper shrimp together. Plate each fish with the pickle poured over and a piece of bammy, and plate the shrimp in a bowl. Then clean and sanitise the area. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the plates are done and the area is clean.
materials: 1 whole fish for each member (such as snapper, about 300–400 g), kept on ice
About 1 kg raw shrimp, kept on ice
Onion, carrot, sweet pepper, cho cho, Scotch bonnet pepper, pimento berries, vinegar, salt, sugar
Garlic, annatto or paprika for the shrimp
Fish scaler, filleting knife, scissors, boards in the Centre's colour for raw fish
Frying pans, oil, slotted spoon, kitchen paper, pots
Clean probe thermometer, disposable gloves, detergent, food-safe sanitiser, cloths
photos: The raw-fish work area set up, with fish and shrimp on ice
Each member's fish scaled, gutted and scored
The pickle vegetables cut into thin strips
A fish being fried, laid in away from the body
The shrimp peeled or deveined, then the cooked pepper shrimp
The finished escovitch fish plates and the shrimp bowl
The work area cleaned and sanitised, with fish waste bagged and binned
checklist: Kept the fish and shrimp on ice or in the fridge until each was used
Scaled from tail to head, gutted, removed the gills and washed the cavity
Scored the fish evenly and patted it dry before frying
Fried the fish safely and until the flesh was opaque and flaked at the bone
Deveined the shrimp neatly and cooked them only until pink and firm
Wore gloves for the hot peppers and made the pickle as the recipe says
Plated neatly, with the pickle over the fish and a clean plate rim
Cleaned and sanitised the boards, knives, sink and bench, and binned the fish waste
safety: Watch for sharp fins and spines when scaling and trimming
Pat the fish dry and lay it into the oil away from you so it does not spit
Never leave hot oil unattended; keep a fire blanket near
Keep raw seafood apart from other food, and wash your hands after handling it
Carry knives point down and wash them straight after use, never leaving them in the sink
